Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients’ personal and health data was compromised during breach

Zack Whittaker

8:00 AM PDT · October 23, 2026

Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators.

Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctors’ offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data.

The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating.

The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Health tech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom.

In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud, Scotland-based health tech provider Craneware, and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson.

The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems.

Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts.

Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. Amanda Rivera, a spokesperson for Quest, did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident and referred to its security notice.

In the notice, Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code, which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.)

This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019.

Do you work at Quest Diagnostics or know more about the data breach? We’d love to hear from you. You can reach this reporter on Signal at the username zackwhittaker.1337 or by email zack.whittaker@techcrunch.com.

The Qilin ransomware group has allegedly listed Premier Medical Group, a US healthcare organization operating at premiermedicalhv.com, on its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the attack was purportedly carried out on October 26, 2026. The group has not disclosed the volume of data it claims to hold, and no data samples or proof-of-compromise artifacts have been publicly referenced in the listing metadata reviewed by Yazoul Security.
This claim remains unverified. Listing a victim on a leak site is a low-cost action for ransomware operators and does not by itself confirm that data was exfiltrated or that encryption occurred. Healthcare organizations are frequently targeted, and false or premature listings do occur.
Threat Actor Profile
qilin is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that has been active since approximately 2022 and is widely tracked under names including “Agenda.” Public reporting from multiple security vendors has associated the group with double extortion tactics, meaning the actor purports to steal data before deploying encryption and then threatens publication to pressure payment.
Qilin has been linked in public research to the use of legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools, as well as credential theft and lateral movement techniques common to RaaS affiliates. Because Qilin operates on an affiliate model, the specific tools and tactics used in any given intrusion can vary significantly between affiliates. Yazoul Security has no independent visibility into the tooling used in this alleged incident, and the group’s total victim count and current toolset are not confirmed in the data reviewed for this report.
No public YARA rules or detection signatures specific to this claim are available at the time of writing. Organizations should rely on general Qilin detection guidance published by established vendors and on behavioral detections for double extortion activity.
Alleged Data Exposure
The leak site entry reportedly does not specify a data volume, data categories, or a ransom demand. No samples, file trees, or credential material have been referenced in the metadata reviewed. As such, there is currently no public basis to assess what, if any, protected health information (PHI) or personally identifiable information (PII) may be involved.
Readers should treat any future claims of “terabytes” or “millions of records” from the actor with skepticism until independently corroborated. Ransomware groups routinely inflate claimed data volumes to increase pressure on victims.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, a healthcare organization of this profile could face risks including operational disruption to clinical systems, exposure of sensitive patient data, regulatory scrutiny under HIPAA, and reputational harm. However, none of these outcomes are confirmed. At this stage, the impact is hypothetical and contingent on verification.
What to Watch For

Official statements from Premier Medical Group or its representatives.
Regulatory filings or breach notifications that would corroborate the claim.
Independent confirmation from incident response firms or law enforcement.
Any published data samples, which Yazoul Security will not link to or reproduce.
Updates to the leak site entry, including countdown timers or added claims.

Organizations in the healthcare sector should review Qilin detection guidance and validate backup integrity and RMM tool controls as a precaution.

text:
Customer experience company Genesys says it has contained a cyberattack that involved unauthorized access to data.

Headquartered in Menlo Park, California, Genesys is a provider of customer experience and call center technology for mid-sized and large organizations.

On October 19, the company announced that hackers had accessed internal business systems, including a learning management system (LMS) and a customer relationship management (CRM) environment.

The Genesys Cloud, Genesys Engage, and Genesys Engage Cloud platforms have not been compromised, and the customer and partner data stored within those systems was not affected, it said.

As part of the incident, the attackers accessed and likely downloaded information such as “business and account information used to manage relationships with existing and prospective customers.”

The potentially compromised data includes names, phone numbers, business email addresses, job titles, company and account information, and other customer interaction information.

Genesys immediately deployed containment measures, which included suspending the LMS platform, and on October 23 announced that the incident has been fully contained.

“We have confirmed that the Genesys Cloud, Genesys Engage and Genesys Engage Cloud platforms were not compromised, and there was no unauthorized access to the platforms, customer and partner environments, or customer and partner data stored or processed within these platforms,” the company said.

On Friday, Genesys said its investigation into the scope and impact of the incident remains ongoing, but promised additional details as it reviews the information accessed and as material facts are confirmed.

The company cautioned customers to watch for suspicious communications impersonating Genesys, stressing that it would never ask customers for sensitive information such as passwords via email or other unsolicited channels.

Genesys has not named the attacker, but a recently emerged group called ScarlettGroup has claimed the attack on its leak site.

A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.

According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.

The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “The Trade Secret,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.

“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”

When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-to-trace cryptocurrency.

ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery firms like MonsterCloud to insurance giants that cover ransom payments, all fueled the extortion economy. Ransomware remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to use ransomware as a cover for espionage. The prevalence of AI tools is also making it easier for attackers to spread ransomware.

Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”

Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.

In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed the firm would never pay a ransom.

Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as well as extensive global contacts.

Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison.

# Contractor risk and the myth of the backup

Forget those news stories about fancy state actors if you want to see a real disaster. Look at the Mos Card mess in Japan. Some contractor left a server wide open and 1.13 million records leaked. Now card numbers and PINs are just floating out there for anyone to find.

Can you imagine the blast radius? Losing an email address is a nuisance, and losing a password is a quick reset. But leaking 1.13 million PINs isn't a digital cleanup job. It is a physical logistics nightmare because you have to kill those cards and mail out new ones. That is one Tuesday that costs more than most companies spend on security in an entire year.

There probably wasn't some complex exploit here. The mistake was giving a contractor the keys to the kingdom without checking where they were kept. We've seen this since the early 2000s. I remember when Code Red hit and caused total chaos. It wasn't just the worm that mattered, it was how many people didn't even know what software was running on their own servers. Twenty six years later, we are still acting surprised when a third party fails at basic hygiene.

Then there is the ConnectWise hit. This is a classic supply chain pivot. The attackers got into the provider and used that bridge to jump into hundreds of Microsoft 365 tenants.

Analysts love using terms like "advanced persistent threats" or "lateral movement." Let's stop that. Most of these moves are just people using a valid credential they found in a plaintext file or an API key that nobody revoked. The real story is the second order effect. It isn't just about ConnectWise getting hit. Every one of those hundreds of tenants has to assume their whole M365 environment is compromised now. Their SharePoint files, emails, and internal chats are all poisoned. If you use a managed service provider but haven't audited your global admin permissions in the last month, you aren't a customer. You're a liability.

It feels like NotPetya all over again. Everyone focused on the Ukrainian accounting software update that started it, but the real damage happened because companies had flat networks and trusted their internal pipes too much. It is the exact same thing. Once the provider you trust is compromised, your perimeter doesn't exist anymore.

While you're worrying about who attacked whom, you should be looking at your restore logs.

I saw a piece of data recently that should make every CISO lose sleep: only 28% of organizations actually recover their data from cloud backup services. Let that sink in. Just under a third. That means if you're paying for a "premium" cloud backup solution, there is a north-of-70% chance it won't actually work when the screen goes black and the ransom note appears.

Here is my position: Most companies are practicing security theater with their backups. They love the dashboard that shows a green checkmark next to "Backup Successful." But a successful backup is not a successful restore. I’ve spent two decades walking into server rooms where the "backup" was a tape drive that hadn't been tested since 2014 or a cloud bucket with no one who knew how to trigger a full-site recovery.

The objection you'll hear from the vendors is that they provide "immutable backups" and "point-in-time recovery." That sounds great in a slide deck. But immutability doesn't matter if your identity provider is gone, your DNS is hijacked, and you don't have an offline copy of the encryption keys. You can have an immutable pile of data that is completely useless because you have no environment to restore it into.

If you want to survive a breach, stop asking who did it. I don't care if it was a teenager in a basement or a government agency. I care about how fast we can get the database back online without paying a cent to a criminal.

text:
Illustration of the idea in the article: two breach notices read with the same list of questions. Conceptual. The logos are shown for identification and the picture claims nothing beyond the article.

Two breach notices in one week, from a game company and a bank. The same six questions show what each one confirms, what it does not, and what you should do.

The headline number is rarely the number that matters

A breach notice tells you what the company has confirmed so far, in the words its lawyers chose, and the gaps are part of the message.

In the week of 19 October 2026, two organizations disclosed that customer data had been taken. Capcom, the Japanese game maker, reported unauthorized access to its CAPCOM ID account system. State Bank of India, SBI, told its stock exchanges in a filing on 21 October that it had experienced “an incident involving the loss of certain data.”

This article is for anyone who gets a breach email, supports people who do, or has to write one someday. It uses these two notices to teach six questions that work on any notice. It does not tell the story of an attack, because neither organization has said how the attack happened.

Question 1: What is being counted?

Capcom says 11,774,247 records worldwide had email addresses and some system identifiers exposed. Some news headlines turned that into 11.7 million accounts.

A record is one row of data, such as one account. It is not always one person, because one person can hold several accounts. The numbers are close, but they are not the same thing.

SBI shows the same problem in a different shape. Its filing says a preliminary analysis of about 375,000 records available on the dark web found 3,897 customer records containing personal information.

The 375,000 is roughly the size a criminal seller advertised. The 3,897 is what the bank says it has identified so far. They answer different questions, and neither tells you how many people are affected.

Question 2: Which fields were taken?

The field list tells you the risk, so read it slowly. Capcom lists email addresses, account creation time, last login time, login count and the network address used at the last login. For 43 records it also lists date of birth, gender, country or region, and nickname. Capcom says credit card information is not included.

SBI’s filing says the exposed information “reportedly included” names, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, gender, email and home addresses, branch and customer (CIF) identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata about loan and lead records. It does not list account numbers, balances, passwords or card details. That is a reassuring absence, but a name, a phone number and a loan detail are plenty for a convincing phone call. Capcom itself warns that the data could be used in phishing emails that pretend to be Capcom.

Question 3: Was data read, changed, or both?

Capcom says passwords were changed without authorization on 196 accounts, and that it has reset them. It says it has not confirmed any leak of passwords that customers set. Those are two separate facts, and the notice keeps them apart.

Our reading is that changing a password means the intruder could write to the account system, and not only read from it. Capcom does not say that. It is an inference from the fact, and a good reason to ask what else the access allowed.

Question 4: When did it start and when was it found?

Notices usually give a detection date and are quiet about the start. Capcom says it found suspicious activity on 19 October, set up a response team on 20 October, told the police and Japan’s data protection regulator on 21 October, and published its statement on 22 October. It does not say when the attackers first got in.

SBI’s timeline is shorter on detail and different in kind. SBI’s filing says the bank received alerts on 16 October from three senders, its threat intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In, about the suspected exposure of customer data on […]

The ransomware group known as emperador has allegedly listed AB InBev, the Belgium-headquartered global brewing conglomerate, on its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the attack was purportedly carried out on October 25, 2026, targeting the domain ab-inbev.be. The group claims to hold a variety of data and is demanding $1,000,000 in Bitcoin.
This report is based entirely on the unverified claim published by the threat actor. Yazoul Security has not independently confirmed the breach, the data, or the demand. Readers should treat all specifics below as allegations until corroborated by the organization or a trusted third party.
Threat Actor Profile
emperador is a relatively low-profile ransomware operation. At the time of writing, there is no public research available on the group’s tooling, infrastructure, or historical victim count. The actor’s total known victims are listed as unknown, and its known tools are likewise undocumented in open sources.
Because emperador lacks a documented track record, its credibility cannot be reliably assessed. Groups with little public history sometimes exaggerate data volumes, inflate victim significance, or reuse leaked material from prior incidents to manufacture leverage. The absence of established tooling signatures also means defenders have no confirmed indicators of compromise to hunt against. Until independent research emerges, treat emperador as an unproven actor whose claims warrant skepticism. No YARA rules or detection guidance specific to this group are currently available.
Alleged Data Exposure
According to the threat actor, the purported dataset totals approximately 3.2GB and allegedly includes:

329,244 “social-listening alerts”
2,510 corporate emails across subsidiaries
19,000 access logs
GBS portal records
Internal PKI certificates
3.2GB of Azure blob assets

The group’s demand is purportedly $1,000,000 in BTC. Notably, the claimed “social-listening alerts” and access logs are the kind of material that can be scraped or aggregated rather than exfiltrated from core systems, which raises questions about the true sensitivity and provenance of the alleged data. The mention of internal PKI certificates, if accurate, would be the most consequential element, but this remains unverified.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, potential impacts could include exposure of internal communications, authentication-related material, and cloud storage contents. PKI certificate exposure, if genuine, could theoretically enable impersonation or trust abuse, though certificate revocation and rotation are standard mitigations. Reputational and regulatory exposure is plausible given AB InBev’s scale and Belgian and EU data protection obligations.
However, ransomware groups routinely overstate their access to pressure victims into fast payment. The blend of marketing-style data (“social-listening alerts”) with technical artifacts suggests the actor may be padding its claim. No impact should be assumed confirmed.
What to Watch For

Official statement from AB InBev or its subsidiaries confirming or denying the incident.
Regulatory notifications under GDPR or Belgian authority guidance.
Certificate transparency or revocation activity tied to AB InBev infrastructure.
Emergence of independent research on emperador’s tooling and tactics.
Any leak site updates, countdowns, or sample releases by the actor.

Organizations in retail, manufacturing, and food production should review third-party and cloud access controls and monitor for credential reuse.

Ralentir l’IA ? Ce que le débat sur le moratoire dit du pari économique américain

Citer

Ajouter aux favoris

Camille Boulenguer

Chercheuse à l’IRIS, directrice de l’Observatoire géopolitique du numérique et des technologies émergentes

Le 12 septembre 2026, Dario Amodei, cofondateur et directeur général d’Anthropic, a appelé à ralentir le développement des modèles les plus avancés, après des incidents au cours desquels des essaims d’agents autonomes ont mené des cyberattaques contre des cibles étrangères à leur tâche. Sam Altman (OpenAI) et Elon Musk (xAI) ont aussitôt soutenu la démarche, OpenAI s’engageant à son tour à accueillir des évaluateurs indépendants. Réseaux sociaux et médias ont alors diffusé des scénarios dystopiques d’une IA échappant au contrôle humain et prenant, à brève échéance, le contrôle de la planète. Les incidents rapportés relèvent plus prosaïquement de la difficulté à évaluer et à superviser des agents capables d’agir de manière autonome dans des environnements numériques.

Reste à savoir de quoi cet appel est le nom. S’agit-il d’une mesure de précaution face aux risques des agents autonomes, d’un instrument de régulation pour reprendre la main sur une course devenue difficile à gouverner, ou d’une stratégie concurrentielle dans la conquête des marchés, des talents et des capacités de calcul ?

La controverse révèle un problème plus général de coordination dans le temps. Les partisans d’un ralentissement estiment que le développement technologique et l’investissement industriel vont désormais plus vite que les mécanismes d’évaluation, de contrôle et de régulation. Leurs opposants jugent qu’un ralentissement aurait un coût stratégique et compromettrait l’avance des États-Unis. Le débat porte donc autant sur le niveau de risque acceptable que sur le rythme auquel une société peut absorber une innovation dont les investissements, les usages, les effets économiques et l’encadrement réglementaire ne progressent pas au même pas. Dans quelle mesure la controverse sur le moratoire révèle-t-elle les fragilités du pari économique américain sur l’IA, et quels effets de concentration ce décalage, ou sa régulation, peut-il produire ?

Dans quelle mesure la controverse sur le moratoire révèle-t-elle les fragilités du pari économique américain sur l’IA, et quels effets de concentration ce décalage, ou sa régulation, peut-il produire ?

Cette note défend trois hypothèses :

La fragilité du système tient d’abord moins à l’inexactitude des anticipations qu’au décalage entre plusieurs temporalités économiques et institutionnelles.

Les montages financiers de l’écosystème de l’IA ne suppriment pas le risque : ils le déplacent entre acteurs, et une part croissante pourrait en être assumée, directement ou non, par la puissance publique.

Enfin, les économies d’échelle et la rivalité entre grandes puissances, que la guerre rend concrète, rendent le ralentissement rationnel collectivement mais coûteux pour chaque acteur, ce qui pousse à poursuivre l’accumulation de capacités malgré l’incertitude sur les débouchés.

L’objet n’est pas de trancher l’existence d’une bulle technologique. Quels que soient l’issue des controverses réglementaires et le rythme de diffusion de l’IA, les mécanismes à l’œuvre favorisent les acteurs les mieux dotés en ressources financières, énergétiques, réglementaires et infrastructurelles. La dynamique observée est, en ce sens, structurellement concentratrice, quel que soit le scénario retenu.

title: Du renseignement réservé au renseignement partagé : vers une intelligence économique distribuée
text:
Du renseignement réservé au renseignement partagé : vers une intelligence économique distribuée

par Didier Arbant et Laurent Muller (fondateurs de Reticular Project).
Depuis le rapport Martre, en 1994, l’intelligence économique est définie comme une démarche collective  et continue. Dans les faits, trente ans plus tard, sa mise en œuvre reste bien souvent tributaire d’une organisation verticale avec des spécialistes qui collectent, analysent puis transmettent à un petit cercle de décideurs.
Le paradoxe : une intelligence économique collective dans les principes, cloisonnée dans les pratiques
Ce modèle n’est pas dépourvu de mérites, mais il laisse subsister un paradoxe : les entreprises disposent d’une quantité croissante d’informations sur leur environnement et consacrent des moyens conséquents à mesurer leur propre activité. Pour autant, les dirigeants qui ont quotidiennement à prendre des décisions ne disposent pas toujours d’éléments éclairant qui leur seraient utiles. Plus encore, des faits collectés au contact des clients, des fournisseurs, des territoires se transmettent de façon informelle, au gré des échanges interpersonnels.
L’expérience opérationnelle et le choix du renseignement ouvert
Nos parcours nous ont conduits à exercer des responsabilités opérationnelles, respectivement dans les secteurs public et privé, puis à intervenir comme prestataires de renseignement pour de grands groupes. Nous avons pratiqué différentes formes de recherche et de collecte, de l’ouvert au gris et au noir.
Cette expérience nous a progressivement amenés à nous forger une conviction : le principal gisement de productivité du renseignement économique ne réside pas nécessairement dans l’information la plus difficile à obtenir, mais dans l’exploitation méthodique d’une information déjà accessible, abondante et insuffisamment valorisée.
Le renseignement de sources ouvertes présente à cet égard une caractéristique décisive : il peut être collecté et traité à grande échelle, puis distribué et réutilisé au bénéfice de nombreux métiers. Quand l’identification des sources humaines, leur approche et leur traitement requiert d’importantes allocations de ressources et une patience infinie, le renseignement économique ouvert et le développement des réseaux sociaux et des données accessibles en ligne offrent des opportunités infinies. De surcroit, l’IA simplifie grandement le traitement des sources numériques en démocratisant l’analyse sémantique multilingue.
Changer de modèle : de la remontée hiérarchique à la circulation du renseignement
Le commandement par l’intention, élaboré dans la tradition militaire prussienne, repose sur un constat simple : celui qui se trouve au contact de la situation dispose souvent d’informations plus récentes et plus précises que son supérieur hiérarchique. Dès lors que l’objectif et l’intention générale sont compris, l’acteur de terrain doit pouvoir adapter son action sans attendre de nouvelles instructions.
Plus récemment, le général Stanley McChrystal a prolongé cette logique avec son modèle Team of Teams, qui associe une compréhension partagée de la situation à une exécution décentralisée. Appliquée à l’entreprise, cette conception invite à repenser la circulation du renseignement. Celui-ci ne devrait pas uniquement remonter vers un centre décisionnel avant de redescendre sous forme d’instructions. Il devrait circuler entre les différentes fonctions, chacune recevant les informations nécessaires à son activité et contribuant en retour à la connaissance collective.
La métaphore du système circulatoire nous paraît ici plus pertinente que celle du système nerveux. Les organes ne fonctionnent pas en adressant continuellement leurs besoins au cerveau. Ils bénéficient d’une circulation permanente de ressources et participent à l’équilibre de l’ensemble. L’entreprise pourrait s’inspirer de cette logique sans renoncer à l’unité de direction.

Now, as Chancellor, he must decide whether to commit to reaching 3% by 2030 – meaning increasing defence spending faster than current plans – and, if so, where any additional money is to come from.Defence spending has increased substantially in recent years. Existing plans imply that NATO-qualifying spending (a broad measure including most Ministry of Defence spending, along with military pensions and some spending on intelligence agencies) will reach 2.7% of GDP by 2027–28, up from 2.1% in 2023–24. But there is clear pressure for the UK to go further and faster. The government has committed to spend 3% of GDP on defence at some point in the next parliament, and 3.5% by 2035 alongside NATO Allies. (NATO Allies also committed to spend an extra 1.5% of GDP on wider 'resilience and security' by 2035, but the government has suggested this would be met within pre-existing spending plans, so here we focus on 'core' defence spending.)While the UK has increased spending considerably, some other NATO countries have moved further and faster. Poland spent a similar share of GDP on defence to the UK four years ago, but by 2025 had increased defence spending to 4.3% of GDP. Germany is also planning to increase defence spending faster than the UK, and overtook the UK as having the second -largest defence budget in NATO in 2024.Further increases could be expensive. Even before any new commitments, the government still needs to find an average of £1.2 billion per year to fully fund top-ups announced alongside the Defence Investment Plan in June. Reaching 3% of GDP on defence by 2030–31 would require around £11 billion of additional spending in that year, relative to keeping defence spending at 2.7% of GDP. Going further to 3.5% would require an even larger, and more sustained, increase.The central question – at both this Budget and next year's Spending Review – is how the government will reconcile its defence ambitions with an already-challenging fiscal outlook, a commitment to reduce the size of the deficit and substantial pressures to increase spending on other public services. AI slop is piling up highest on the biggest open-source projects

The maintainers of large open source projects are taking the worst of the AI slop. In a Linux Foundation survey of 234 open source contributors and maintainers, people running projects with more than 50 contributors estimated that close to a third of the code changes landing in their queue are low quality or AI-generated. Those maintainers now worry more about burning out than about the code itself.

Across all projects, the estimate comes to about one in four. Each of those submissions, called a pull request, has to be read by a person before it gets merged or rejected. That person is a maintainer, and every piece of junk in the queue takes time away from the work that keeps the project running.
Bigger projects, bigger pile
You’d think a large project could spread the extra load across more reviewers. It doesn’t work out that way. Large projects reported the most slop, the fastest growth in submissions, and the most complaints about reviews dragging on.
Most maintainers say they’re getting more contributions since generative AI took off. Smaller projects still rank code quality as their main worry about AI-assisted work. On the big ones, burnout has moved to the top of the list.
Few projects have rules yet
About a third of projects have a formal policy that allows AI-assisted contributions, and one in ten bans them. The rest either have nothing written down or are still working on it. Where policies do exist, they mostly ask contributors to disclose AI use and to take responsibility for reviewing their own work.
Without rules, maintainers check AI-assisted code the old-fashioned way. They trust contributors they know, or they read the code themselves, and about a quarter have no check in place at all. Plenty are also fighting fire with fire. Three in four maintainers use AI tools to help vet what comes in, usually to summarize a change or hunt for logic bugs.
Contributors say they’re careful
The picture from the developer side is better than you might expect. Six in ten say they go through AI-generated code line by line and test it fully before submitting. Very few admit to sending it in unchecked.
Contributors are much less consistent about telling anyone AI was involved. About one in five never mention it. If you run a project and want a standard to point people to, the Linux kernel already asks for an “Assisted-by:” line in commit messages that names the AI tool and model used.
The time savings are real, up to a point
People who use AI say it roughly halves the time they spend writing code and cuts review time by more than 40%. Those savings shrink as the work gets harder. On the most complex tasks, about one in five developers say AI slows them down.
There’s a cost on the community side too. Most maintainers agree that AI makes it easier for newcomers to get involved. More than half say it hasn’t done anything for trust within their community. More of them say new contributors need extra mentoring than say they need less, and that mentoring falls on the same maintainers already handling the bigger queue.
The curl project shows that the problem can ease. In 2025, project lead Daniel Stenberg described curl as overwhelmed by AI slop in its vulnerability reports. By April 2026, he said the project had “stopped getting AI slop security reports” and was getting “an ever-increasing amount of really good security reports, almost all done with the help of AI.”

OpenSSL 4.1.0: What’s new, what’s removed, and what’s still broken

The OpenSSL project released version 4.1.0, adding support for DTLS 1.3 and listing four known bugs in the DTLS code that ships with it. DTLS is the variant of TLS built for datagram transports such as UDP, and version 1.3 is defined in RFC 9147.

The bugs fall on developers who adopt DTLS 1.3 or the DTLS support newly added to OpenSSL’s SSL listener API. Two of them can make an application misread a connection’s state. A permanent receive failure on a DTLS listener can surface as SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ, the code that tells a program to wait for more data, and polling and later accept calls may miss the error too, leaving the application waiting on a dead connection. A retryable write failure on a nonblocking accepted connection can surface as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL, and an application that treats that code as fatal may close a connection that still works.
Handshakes and tickets can go missing
A DTLS 1.3 server may abort a handshake with an unexpected_message alert when the client acknowledges part or all of the server’s first flight before replying. That can happen after packet loss.
The fourth bug involves KeyUpdate, the message a peer sends to switch to fresh encryption keys mid-session. When OpenSSL receives one, it drops all other outstanding post-handshake records from its retransmission buffer. If a NewSessionTicket, which lets a client resume the session later, was lost on its first trip, OpenSSL will not send it again. The project has a fix in progress for this bug and lists no fix status for the other three, so if you run a DTLS 1.3 server, plan around all four.
Build flags that did not do their job
OpenSSL also removed the no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure because they did not really disable the implementations they named. A build configured with either flag still carried the code it was meant to leave out. The project points users to no-ec, which disables elliptic curve support entirely.
Two other changes can break existing setups. OpenSSL dropped the Windows-on-Itanium and Windows CE build targets, and the tsget time-stamping utility now requires the Perl module Net::Curl::Easy, replacing the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy. Anyone who relies on tsget should install the new module before upgrading.
Faster post-quantum math
ML-KEM and ML-DSA, the post-quantum key exchange and signature algorithms, get optimized NTT operations on ppc64le, and ML-DSA gets further x86_64 work that includes AVX-512 SHAKE x4 code. AES-CBC decryption on x86_64 picks up AVX-512 and VAES optimizations. The release also adds RFC 8701 GREASE, which sends random reserved values in handshakes to flush out servers that mishandle values they do not recognize, along with an IKEv2 key derivation function and initial support for the Elbrus2000 architecture.
The DTLS 1.3 guide ships as the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page. Code that accepts connections from a DTLS listener should not take SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ or SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL at face value until OpenSSL fixes those two bugs.

Synthetic identities leave US lenders with $2.4 billion in fraud exposure

Criminals are exploiting established customer accounts and familiar brands to steal money and personal information, according to TransUnion’s Fraud in the Age of Continuous Trust report. Eighty-one percent of suspected digital fraud in its network during the first half of 2026 occurred during account logins and financial transactions, highlighting risks that persist throughout a customer relationship.
Verifying someone’s identity does not establish whether every subsequent interaction can be trusted. Scammers can manipulate legitimate customers into authorizing fraudulent activity, while fabricated identities that pass onboarding checks can be used across multiple services to obtain credit or facilitate further fraud.

Percentage of business leaders who said their organizations are least prepared to manage each fraud type (Source: TransUnion)

A familiar name on the phone
Impersonation scams often begin with a message or call that appears to come from a bank, insurer or healthcare provider. Criminals disguise the sender’s identity and exploit the organization’s reputation to encourage a response.
The request may sound like a routine security procedure: confirm personal details, share a one-time passcode or reset account credentials. Following those instructions can help an attacker take over an account. Fraudsters may also impersonate legitimate representatives to persuade customers to redirect payments.
These exchanges can take place through communication networks outside a business’s direct control. They can shape a customer’s behavior before fraud checks have an opportunity to intervene.
Scams and authorized fraud were the most commonly cited leading source of business fraud losses, selected by 29% of surveyed fraud and risk decision-makers at large consumer-facing organizations across eight markets. Such schemes can involve manipulating a victim into authorizing fraudulent activity, including a transfer of money.
Fake identities spread across services
Criminals use exposed personal information and AI to construct convincing synthetic identities and fabricated documents. Data breaches provide authentic identity details that can help these creations pass verification.
Once accepted, a synthetic identity can be used across several services. A single identity might be used to obtain a buy now, pay later loan, open a mobile phone account with a handset lease, secure a credit card and create an online betting account.
That activity creates risks beyond the initial application. A fabricated identity that slips past onboarding controls can remain undetected as criminals exploit accounts and business processes.
US lenders had an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure to synthetic identity fraud risk at the end of June 2026. Auto lending accounted for the largest portion, at $1.5 billion. These estimates measure potential lender losses, instead of losses already incurred.
AI reduces the work behind an attack
AI can help criminal groups generate documents, write impersonation messages, create identities and target victims. Automating these tasks reduces the effort required to prepare, repeat and adapt a scheme.
The same operation can draw on stolen credentials, fabricated records and recognizable branding to approach people through different services. Successful attacks can extract funds, credit, merchandise or digital goods. Criminal networks can then move the proceeds through synthetic or legitimate accounts, transfers and resale channels.

Forgotten AI agents may still access sensitive company data

AI agents that have not run recently retain credentials and connections to company systems, according to Arrakis Security’s 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report. About 76% of enabled agents examined had not run in 60 days, leaving access available through inactive software.

Agents by exposure family (Source: Arrakis Security)

The analysis covered thousands of agents in customer production environments over a 12-week period. These programs can read and write data, call tools and start workflows, giving them the ability to perform tasks across business services.
“When an agent stops being used, nobody removes anything, because in most companies nobody owns it,” said Tal Baron, CEO of Arrakis Security.
Dormant agents retain working access
Inactivity was measured from each agent’s last recorded run. Forty-four percent had not run in 180 days. Some agents operate on weekly, monthly or quarterly schedules, making the inactivity period relevant to their classification.
About a quarter of dormant agents could still be started through an unsigned webhook from outside the organization.
Unsecured triggers accept requests an agent cannot verify. In some cases, anyone who knows the URL can make the agent run. Other exposures included accepting requests from addresses that should be rejected or accepting the same request after it had already been used.
Across the agents examined, 22.9% had at least one unsecured trigger. A dormant agent activated through such a trigger retains the access associated with its stored credentials and connections.
Sensitive connections lack verified data controls
Seventy percent of agents connected to at least one integration classified as sensitive, including cloud storage, AI and large language model services, and marketing platforms. Of those agents, 99.4% had no verified data loss prevention coverage on the sensitive connection.
Excessive permissions were another recorded exposure. Some agents held connections with broad permissions or access to data with different sensitivity levels. Nineteen percent used API keys and tokens that never expired and were embedded in their configurations.
The analysis identified agents with administrative privileges and connections to services outside their listed integrations.
Agents delegate work across systems
Some agents could send content to a model operated by a third party and use its answer to determine the next step. Others could pass a task to another agent running under its own credentials.
The initiating agent receives output produced using another agent’s permissions, without any transfer of permissions.
Behavioral exposures covered actions taken during execution, including revealing an agent’s own instructions or sending requests to destinations supplied through tool descriptions. These were recorded separately from configuration and access problems.
Hugging Face incident involved agent coordination
A separate METR investigation into the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident documented agents communicating and participating in activity beyond their assigned tasks during OpenAI’s ExploitGym evaluations.
In an investigation published on August 26, 2026, researchers described how about 1,200 agents intended to operate in isolation found a way to communicate through an unauthorized message board. They exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files. Approximately 700 subsequently participated in the Hugging Face attack.

A single hacked device on a Tailscale network can be used to gain root access to other servers it can reach, according to a security researcher who published the findings this week.

The attack requires two things: Tailscale SSH set up to allow port forwarding, and an attacker who already controls one device that the network's access rules permit to connect to the target.

The findings were published on October 25 in a report called Tailworm by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs. Windisch tested Tailscale version 1.104.2 and headscale version 0.29.5, the self-hosted server some networks use to run Tailscale instead of the company's hosted service, over three days in a lab.

The report describes tests on that software, not attacks against real networks. As of publication, Tailscale had issued no security bulletin, no CVE identifier, and no fixed version.

Tailscale has responded in public. Mike Shaver, the company's vice president of engineering, wrote on Reddit that Tailscale had received the report, had already been looking at the same areas with outside security specialists, and had found issues it is working to fix. Shaver said the company is still working out which setups are affected, and that it is "not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH."

Tailscale SSH does not work like a normal SSH server. Rather than checking a connecting user's password or key, it identifies the device, and a single access rule decides whether that device may open an SSH session to a target.

Because of this, the attack needs no stolen passwords or keys. It needs a foothold on one device first, which the report says an attacker can get the usual ways: a vulnerable web application, a poisoned software package, phishing, or stolen login details. Tailscale does not create that first foothold.

How much an administrator can do about it depends on where the network is run. On Tailscale's hosted service, forwarding can be switched off per rule. On headscale version 0.29.5, forwarding cannot be turned off at all. The report says every SSH grant there should therefore be treated as giving root on the target.

In the lab, Windisch showed the problem in stages. Using standard SSH port forwarding, an ordinary session caused the root-level Tailscale process to connect to a system socket that only root should access, and the test gained root and read the system password file almost immediately, without administrator rights.

A second method replaced a root-owned socket with the attacker's, allowing direct root command execution against certain services.

A third method defeated a safety check meant to limit which files forwarding can access by racing the system between when it checks a file path and when it uses it. That chain went further in the lab, the report says: it captured a key used to enroll new devices and used the key to join an attacker's own machine to the network as a trusted server.

That last step worked from start to finish only on networks where Tailscale's Tailnet Lock feature was not enabled. On networks that do, the needed secrets were captured in transit, but the final step was not completed.

Windisch describes the overall result as "wormable." In the lab, one compromised device could spread to every device that the access rules allow, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

In the report's words, "the mesh converts one ordinary foothold into fleet-wide privileged access at machine speed." That spread was measured in a lab, not seen on real networks.

A malicious instruction file sitting in a developer's Downloads folder tried to make their AI coding agent install a known-malicious npm package, security firm Forever Security said in a report published last week.

The company caught the attempt on a real customer's machine and stopped the agent before any code ran. It could not determine how the file got into the folder.

The file was AGENTS.md, a plain-text instructions file that a coding agent, such as OpenAI's Codex, reads when it starts in a folder and follows as directions.

It was dressed up as ordinary engineering notes. One section told the agent to add a server to its own configuration and install a package called function-color from npm.

That package is part of a malware campaign that other researchers have documented separately: function-color pulls in a downloader called function-flag, which fetches and runs a Windows payload. Researchers at CloudSEK and Checkmarx, who analyzed the campaign, named it MALFEX.

Two things, each harmless on its own, make this work, Forever said. An agent is built to trust and obey the instructions file in the folder it opens. And a web page can save a file to the Downloads folder on its own, without a click or a permission prompt, choosing the name and contents. Put together, a web page can drop a file the agent will treat as orders into a folder the agent trusts.

Researchers did not establish that this is how the file was caught. To test whether the full path was possible, it built its own proof-of-concept page: visit it, and an AGENTS.md downloads silently into Downloads. Whether a real attacker used that route against the customer is not known.

The firm then reproduced the attack on two coding agents to show that it was not specific to a single product. Against Codex, it ran the real attacker file inside an isolated virtual machine. The file, framed as routine project setup, told Codex to register a server in ~/.codex/config.toml and run a command that installed the package.

Because that config file applies to every Codex session on the machine, the change would load the attacker's server in any folder afterward, not just Downloads. Codex ran the malware in more than 90% of attempts, Forever said.

Against Claude Code, the working attack looked different and succeeded less often. A planted CLAUDE.md, framed as internal gateway setup, tried to make Claude write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL into a project settings file, pointing its API traffic at a server Forever controlled. That one change leaks the session's login token, which is account takeover on its own, and lets the server reply as if it were the model and hand back commands the agent runs.

Claude needs a person to approve a write like that and often refuses one that looks wrong; the long engineering-doc framing got the write approved about half the time, researchers said.

There is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, in Forever's view, because an agent following the instructions file in its folder is doing what it was built to do. The company compared it to a browser rendering a phishing page: the browser worked as designed, and the attack lies in the page. "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch," Forever said.

What to do

Forever's advice is practical and needs no product:

Do not start Codex, Claude Code, or any agent in ~/Downloads. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own.
Look for instructions files you did not write. A stray AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, in Downloads or in a repository you just cloned, is the whole attack. Read it before you let an agent near it.
